headline: NiSource signs 20-year deal with Microsoft for about 1,100 MW of new generation; Microsoft funds the build
players: NiSource announced a long-term energy agreement with Microsoft for its northwest Indiana data centre campus. The 20-year deal starts in 2028 and adds about 1,100 MW of new generation. Microsoft will fully fund all generation and transmission needed to serve its load, through NiSource Generation Company LLC. Pricing was not in the coverage I read.
why_it_matters: The customer pays for the build and signs for 20 years, so the utility takes little ratepayer or stranded-asset risk. That is a template for data-centre load: ring-fenced generation, hyperscaler credit, long tenor. Return terms are not public. Watch for pricing detail, the generation mix and any regulatory filings.
why_you_care: A fresh structure to compare against when you underwrite power or utility assets sold into data-centre demand, though the economics are not yet disclosed.

headline: Venture Global says it is targeting 10 GW of gas-fired power for AI data centres
players: Venture Global is targeting 10 GW of gas-fired power for AI data centres, per OilPrice. The company said any third-party data centre developments would stay separate from its LNG exports and would not affect existing gas supply commitments. Its LNG capacity in production, construction or development exceeds 100 million tonnes a year. I did not open the company release; customers and capital cost were not in the coverage I read.
why_it_matters: A large LNG developer moving into power shows how crowded the behind-the-meter gas market is getting. It could compete with sponsors building the same product, or sell them gas and turbines. A 10 GW target is a goal, not contracted revenue. Watch for named customers, signed offtake and a financing plan.
why_you_care: Adds a well-capitalised competitor to the gas-to-power space MSIP targets, which could squeeze returns on greenfield behind-the-meter projects you may look at.

headline: A.P. Moller Capital agrees to buy Portek International from Mitsui; price not found
players: A.P. Moller Capital announced on Oct 15 that it agreed to buy all shares in Singapore-based Portek International from Japan's Mitsui & Co. The deal runs through its Emerging Markets Infrastructure Fund II. Portek holds interests in seven multipurpose terminals in Algeria, Gabon, Indonesia, Latvia, Malta and Vietnam. It follows A.P. Moller Capital's Sept 28 agreement to take a majority of Euroports; terms of Portek were not found.
why_it_matters: Port terminals give long-dated, volume-linked cash flows, and the buyer says it will work on operations, safety and emissions with local teams. Two port deals in under three weeks, plus an existing Philippine logistics holding, show a sponsor building a ports and logistics book. With no price disclosed, there is no multiple to mark against yet. Watch for closing conditions.
why_you_care: Another sponsor is adding port terminals, which supports the demand side of your LOGISTEC/Termont thesis, though without a price this is background rather than a comp you can mark against.

headline: EQT Q3 report highlights Copia Power and AI infrastructure push; Infrastructure VII due to activate around year-end
players: EQT's Q3 announcement lists the Copia Power acquisition by EQT Infrastructure VII and says its new AI Infrastructure strategy has strong early momentum. The July deal buys Copia from Carlyle and is expected to close by end-2026. IPE understands the price is about $2.6bn; EQT has not disclosed it. Copia has over 2.6 GW operating or under construction and is developing over 9 GW of data centres.
why_it_matters: EQT is paying for interconnection positions where generation and data-centre load sit together, mostly development pipeline rather than cash flow today. Infrastructure VII will be only 0-5% invested after Copia, while the current fund is 75-80% invested, so fresh capital is coming. Watch for the closing, and for IPE's reported $2.6bn price staying unconfirmed.
why_you_care: EQT is going straight at integrated power-plus-data-centre platforms, an area MSIP also covers; the reported $2.6bn for Copia is a marker for what such platforms fetch.

headline: FERC publishes Oct 15 meeting order summaries; accepts 2027 NERC and regional budgets
players: FERC posted summaries of orders voted at its Oct 15 meeting. They include acceptance of 2027 business plans and budgets for NERC, the six Regional Entities and WIRAB, and conditional acceptance of Deseret G&T's market-based rate tariff revisions. The commission also sustained its dismissal of McKenzie Electric's complaint against Basin Electric. The snippet I read did not show results for the Columbia Gulf, Louisiana LNG or Driftwood dockets.
why_it_matters: Mostly routine. The items that can move underwriting are the gas pipeline certificate orders and the five-year oil pipeline index review (docket G-1), which feeds oil pipeline rate changes, but I could not confirm outcomes. Check the full orders before relying on any of them. The reliability technical conference on Oct 21 is the next FERC event.
why_you_care: Largely background today; once the gas certificate and oil index orders are readable, they matter for any midstream or pipeline underwriting at MSIP.

headline: Brookfield Infrastructure unitholders approve BIP/BIPC simplification with about 99.5% support; closing targeted Q4
players: Brookfield Infrastructure Partners reported that unitholders approved two transaction resolutions with about 99.5% support at the Oct 14 special meeting, with 60.13% of units represented. The plan converts BIP and BIPC into a single Canadian listed corporation, BIP Inc., and still needs British Columbia Supreme Court approval. Completion is expected in Q4 2026; I did not find the BIPC shareholder vote result.
why_it_matters: A near-unanimous unitholder vote clears the main hurdle for a structure change at one of the largest listed infrastructure owners. The underlying assets and cash flows do not change; what changes is how investors hold them. If BIPC shareholders vote no, the filing says the deal still completes without the BIPC share exchange. Watch the court hearing and the BIPC result.
why_you_care: Brookfield is a watchlist rival and frequent bidder; this is housekeeping on its listed vehicle rather than a new deal, so treat it as background.

headline: FERC's Oct 15 open meeting agenda now published; lists Columbia Gulf, Louisiana LNG and Driftwood Pipeline gas dockets
players: The Sunshine Act notice for FERC's 1140th meeting, Oct 15 at 10:00 AM, is due in the Federal Register on Oct 14. Items I could see include Columbia Gulf Transmission (CP26-11-000), Louisiana LNG Infrastructure (CP26-537-000) and Driftwood Pipeline (CP17-118-000), plus administrative items AD27-1 and AD27-2. The listing is partial and no outcomes are known. RTO Insider has posted agenda summaries.
why_it_matters: Gas pipeline and LNG certificate orders set the timing and conditions for new takeaway capacity, which feeds into midstream and gas-to-power valuations. The agenda is the first look at what the commission may decide. Watch the orders themselves, since conditions and in-service dates matter more than the headline approval.
why_you_care: Any gas certificate order tomorrow changes timing assumptions for midstream and gas-to-power underwriting; this adds agenda detail to the Oct 15 meeting already logged, with no outcomes yet.

headline: Flex completes acquisition of EPC Power, adding power-conversion and grid-forming kit for AI data centres; price not found
players: Flex (FLEX) completed its acquisition of EPC Power on Oct 14, adding power conversion and grid-forming technology to its Cloud and Power Infrastructure segment. The digest says Flex's technologies support more than 15 GW deployed. The purchase price was not in the source I read.
why_it_matters: Flex bought a maker of power conversion and grid-forming equipment to sell into AI data-centre and grid projects, a sign that strategics are buying the equipment layer of the power build-out. The price was not in the sources I read, so there is no multiple to mark against. Watch whether sponsors chase similar suppliers.
why_you_care: Background only: a strategic buyer, not a fund, paid for data-centre power electronics; with no price disclosed there is no comp to use yet.

headline: Brazil to auction three port terminals Dec 9 with R$582.7m of planned investment; Tecon Santos 10 model still under review
players: Brazil's Ports and Airports Minister Tomé França said on Oct 8 that three port terminals will be auctioned on Dec 9 at B3 in São Paulo, with combined planned investment of R$582.7m. One is the IQI16 dry bulk terminal at Itaqui for fertilisers, a 25-year lease with R$147m of investment. The wider pipeline is R$160bn, including Tecon Santos 10 (R$6.45bn) and the Port of São Sebastião lease (R$3.84bn).
why_it_matters: Long port leases with committed capex give a pipeline of concession-style deals for sponsors with terminal experience. The December auctions are small. Tecon Santos 10 and São Sebastião are the large prizes, and their timing depends on the government settling the Santos auction model. Watch the rules on foreign and shipping-line participation, which set who can bid and how aggressively.
why_you_care: Brazil's port concession pipeline is a pricing and sourcing reference for terminal deals; it follows AD Ports' $835m purchase of CLI, and it is background rather than a direct MSIP or tracked-deal link.

headline: Brookfield CEO Teskey says AI compute and power demand will outrun supply for years; $100bn programme favours fast-build power
players: Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey says the world wants more compute and electricity than it can build and that the gap is structural. Brookfield's $100bn AI infrastructure programme covers data centres, power generation and wider compute. On power it favours technologies that can be deployed quickly: fuel cells, renewables, batteries and nuclear. Source is secondary commentary; I did not see a Brookfield release.
why_it_matters: The largest infrastructure manager is putting a number on AI spend and choosing speed to power over cost. That supports pricing for assets that can connect or generate quickly, such as uprates, fuel cells and batteries, and for powered land. Watch whether other sponsors back the same list and how much of the $100bn is invested rather than targeted.
why_you_care: Brookfield is a main bidder for the AI power and data-centre assets MSIP also looks at, so its stated power mix is a useful marker for what rivals will pay for.

headline: Greater Napanee council backs bigger Hydrostor Quinte project, 500 MW to up to 650 MW, ahead of IESO bid
players: Greater Napanee council voted unanimously on Oct 13 to raise the proposed Quinte Energy Storage Centre from 500 MW to up to 650 MW, with 5,200 MWh of storage. The site grows from 80 to 95 acres, and the annual community benefits fund rises from about $1m to $1.3m. Staff said the increase supports Hydrostor's submission to the IESO Long Lead-Time Capacity Services procurement; an earlier report said the IESO bid closes in November.
why_it_matters: Hydrostor is resizing the project to compete for an Ontario long-term capacity contract, which would be the revenue backbone. A city official said the company felt a larger size would show better to the IESO. The local noise concern from nearby plants is the permitting risk to watch. The IESO outcome is the next real marker for the pipeline.
why_you_care: This is your Hydrostor deal scaling its Ontario pipeline into a November IESO bid, worth flagging if MSIP is looking at contracted long-duration storage.

headline: FTAI Infrastructure to report Q3 on Nov 5, with Long Ridge sale and Port Arthur purchase both pending

sources.name: ScanX (Q3 timing and Port Arthur summary)

players: FTAI Infrastructure said on Oct 13 it will report Q3 2026 results after the Nasdaq close on Nov 5; a secondary source puts the call at 8:00am ET on Nov 6. Two deals are pending: the $1.52bn Long Ridge sale to MARA, and Jefferson's roughly $255m purchase of the Port Arthur terminal and half of an Alberta diluent unit. The Port Arthur release summary cites about $50m of annual EBITDA and a Q4 2026 closing target.
why_it_matters: Two live transactions now shape the equity story: Long Ridge removes the power asset, while Port Arthur is said to more than double Jefferson's adjusted EBITDA. Q3 is the next scheduled update after Long Ridge's close slipped into Q4. Look for closing timing, use of sale proceeds, and how much debt Jefferson takes on to fund the purchase.
why_you_care: Your deal: the Nov 5 print should show whether Long Ridge closes on schedule and how Port Arthur is funded, useful before pitching any carve-out angle at MSIP.

headline: Infralogic: Q3 infrastructure fundraising led by KKR $19.2bn, Partners Group $15bn; nine-month total 39% below 2025
players: Infralogic's 3Q26 report (Oct 13) says KKR Global Infrastructure Investors V led with a $19.2bn close, then Partners Group Direct Infrastructure IV at $15bn and Energy Capital Partners VI at $8.1bn. The nine-month raise is $97.2bn against $159.5bn a year earlier. Infrastructure funds raised $51.3bn in the quarter, flat on 3Q25's $51.4bn, and 17 funds launched, down from 24 in 2Q26.
why_it_matters: Three large closes drove the quarter, while nine-month volume sits 39% below 2025's record. Capital is pooling at the biggest managers, which points to well-funded bidders for large assets and slower going for smaller sponsors. Watch the 17 new launches, down from 24 in 2Q, for how much of the mid-market fund pipeline thins out.
why_you_care: Background for how MSIP's own fundraising and co-invest conversations sit in a market where LPs are favouring the biggest managers.

headline: Enerflex wins 1 GW+ gas power order for a data centre, after 450 MW award on Oct 1; backlog about 1.75 GW
players: Enerflex said it won a contract to supply more than 1 GW of behind-the-meter, gas-fired power units for an unnamed North American data centre development. It follows the roughly 450 MW award announced Oct 1. Hart Energy puts the data-centre power backlog at 1.75 GW, with deliveries running into the latter part of the decade. Contract value was not found.
why_it_matters: Developers are buying on-site gas generation to avoid grid queues, and orders are now gigawatt-sized. The equipment maker gets one-off manufacturing revenue; the long-term cash flows sit with whoever owns and runs the units. Watch who the end customer is and whether owner-operators sign power contracts behind these orders.
why_you_care: A demand marker for the gas-to-AI power theme you worked on with Sisu/Miratech, and for any MSIP power or gas deal that sells behind the meter.

headline: I Squared Capital hires a new managing director, per Infrastructure Investor's Oct 12 newsletter; details paywalled
players: Infrastructure Investor's start-of-week Pipeline briefing on Oct 12 lists an I Squared Capital managing director hire among its three lead items. The name, team, region and previous employer sit behind the subscriber wall and I did not see them. No deal terms apply.
why_it_matters: A senior hire at a direct rival shows where it is adding capacity, and the sector or region of the hire is the useful part. I could not read that, so this is only a flag. Check the full note or a market contact before drawing any conclusion about I Squared's priorities or a possible move from another firm.
why_you_care: I Squared is one of MSIP's three named rivals; the hire's focus could show where it is pushing next, but the details are unread, so treat it as a lead to check.

headline: NMDC Group inaugurates 148m cutter suction dredger Abu Al Bakhoush in Nantong, China; no financial terms
players: NMDC Group's dredging and marine unit inaugurated the Abu Al Bakhoush, a self-propelled heavy-duty cutter suction dredger, at a ceremony in Nantong. The vessel has a 7.8 MW cutter and 30,040 kW of installed power. It joins a fleet of more than 170 vessels and marine units. UAE Minister of State for Foreign Trade Thani Al Zeyoudi attended. No cost or contract terms were given in the sources I read.
why_it_matters: The group is adding dredging capacity to chase larger international coastal, port and offshore jobs, which supports its marine construction order book. The sources give no contract value, utilisation or vessel cost, so this does not move valuation. Watch for the project awards that would fill the new capacity.
why_you_care: Background only: a fleet milestone at NMDC Group with no deal terms and no direct read-through to the McDermott situation you worked on.

headline: FERC accepts Duke's 75%, 15-year minimum-payment floor for large-load transmission customers
players: In docket ER26-2691, FERC accepted terms Duke wrote into its standard network transmission service agreement. A customer serving a large load must pay for at least 75% of its planned load for 15 years, even if actual load comes in lower. The order also makes rolled-in pricing the default for network upgrades that large loads drive. Commissioner Lindsay See concurred on Oct 9 and urged Duke to use the higher incremental rate where policy allows. She said the order does not prejudge the June 2026 large-load show-cause cases.
why_it_matters: A 75% take-or-pay for 15 years is a concrete, FERC-approved floor on large-load demand. It cuts stranded-cost risk for utilities and for generation built to serve data centres. Rolled-in upgrade pricing still spreads some cost to other customers, and a commissioner called the floor the low end. Expect pressure for tighter terms. Watch the Oct 15 open meeting and the Oct 21 reliability conference.
why_you_care: A 75%, 15-year payment floor is a live reference point when you test load and take-or-pay assumptions on powered-land, data-centre or utility-linked deals at MSIP.

headline: Bloomberg: H.I.G. Capital sounds out investors on about $2.6bn for second infrastructure fund
players: Miami-based H.I.G. Capital is looking to raise about $2.6bn for H.I.G. Infrastructure Partners II, according to people familiar with the matter. The firm has started sounding out existing investors. The report snippet I read gave no strategy, hard cap or launch date.
why_it_matters: This is early-stage: soundings only, with nothing formally launched. At about $2.6bn it is far smaller than LS Power's roughly $6bn Fund VI or Meridiam's $4.5bn North America Core Fund, both closed this month. Another mid-market sponsor is stocking up, which means more competition for smaller deals. Watch for a formal launch and a target.
why_you_care: One more mid-market buyer likely to bid against you on smaller platform deals once this fund is live; background for sizing the competitive field.

headline: DOE tells FERC PJM's stalled 6.8 GW backstop must make data centres pay; PJM plans refiling by Oct 29
players: The US Department of Energy told FERC on Oct 7 that PJM must rework its Reliability Backstop Procurement so data centres, not existing customers, bear the cost of the 6.8 GW shortfall. The report, citing Utility Dive, says it appears to be DOE's first filing of this kind at FERC in at least five years. PJM plans a special Members Committee meeting on Oct 22 and aims to refile by Oct 29.
why_it_matters: This follows FERC's Sept 29 decision to accept the backstop but suspend it to Feb 28, 2027. The cost-allocation fight decides who funds new capacity. If large loads carry the bill, that supports contracted, load-backed generation and weakens the case for socialised capacity payments. Watch the Oct 22 meeting and the Oct 29 refiling.
why_you_care: The outcome sets who pays for new PJM capacity, which affects revenue assumptions on any gas, nuclear or storage asset you mark against, and the cost side of data-centre deals.

headline: FERC rejects PJM's curtail-first plan for new large loads; keeps only 50 MW definition and a load registry
players: FERC ruled on Oct 9 in docket ER26-3515-000. It rejected PJM's Interim Resource Adequacy Service, which would have let a new data centre connect before matching capacity existed, with PJM able to curtail it first. It also rejected the 'bring your own new capacity' rules. It accepted only the 50 MW large-load definition and a registry of each large load's location, ramp schedule and capacity supply. PJM had filed Aug 13 and asked for an Oct 12 effective date.
why_it_matters: FERC's objection was jurisdiction, not the idea: it said the proposal put obligations on retail customers and chose who gets curtailed, which belongs to states. That leaves PJM with no fast-connect route for new data centres. Self-supply and co-located power deals look more valuable as a result. Watch PJM's next filing and which states act on curtailment.
why_you_care: A clear pricing and risk input for any PJM generation or data-centre power case you underwrite: the quick grid-connection route for large loads is gone for now.

headline: FERC calendar: open meeting Oct 15 and commissioner-led reliability technical conference Oct 21
players: FERC's calendar lists an Oct 15 open meeting and a commissioner-led reliability technical conference on Oct 21; it also announced its 2027 commission meeting schedule on Oct 1. Background: after its June 18 open meeting, FERC issued show-cause orders to the six regional grid operators on how large loads such as data centres connect and pay for the grid.
why_it_matters: These are the next scheduled points where FERC can move on grid reliability and large-load rules, which drive how fast data-centre-linked power assets get connected and what they can charge. Co-location and behind-the-meter treatment are among the reform areas FERC has asked grid operators to address. Watch the Oct 15 agenda and what the Oct 21 conference says on supply adequacy.
why_you_care: Dates to diarise before marking power or co-location assumptions: rule changes on large-load interconnection feed straight into MSIP's power and digital underwriting.

headline: HD Hyundai Construction Equipment wins ~$276m deal to supply gas engines to ERock for US hyperscale data-centre power
players: HD Construction Equipment said on Oct 7 it signed a contract worth about 390bn won ($276m) to supply gas-fuelled power-generation engines to ERock, a US power infrastructure solutions provider. Supply runs 2027 to 2028. The product is a 22-litre engine 'long block'; ERock plans to build generator sets for hyperscale data centres run by US Big Tech.
why_it_matters: Grid-connection delays are pushing data centres towards on-site gas generation, and this order shows the equipment chain is being booked for 2027-28, not just the power contracts. For owners of on-site power, engine availability and price become a cost and timing risk in underwriting. Watch who ERock's end customers are and whether other engine makers sign similar deals.
why_you_care: A supply-side data point for any behind-the-meter gas or distributed power case you underwrite at MSIP, including engine lead times and capex assumptions.

headline: Brookfield's minority stake in data-centre developer AREP, announced Sept 16, extends its AI push into powered land; terms undisclosed
players: Brookfield affiliates agreed to buy a minority interest in American Real Estate Partners (AREP), announced Sept 16; stake size and price were not disclosed. Closing is expected in Q4 2026, and Rothschild & Co is advising AREP. AREP's PowerHouse Data Centers platform says it has 140 data centres underway or in planning, nearly 10 GW of potential capacity.
why_it_matters: A minority stake leaves AREP running its own platform while giving Brookfield a route into powered land and entitlements without paying for the whole business. No price is disclosed, so there is no comp to mark. The roughly 10 GW pipeline is development-stage, so value rests on securing power and tenants. Watch for the stake size when it closes in Q4.
why_you_care: A competitor moving up the chain into powered land is a read-across for MSIP's digital book, and it is a deal Rothschild colleagues advised.

headline: Brightline's planned Cocoa station still expected to open in 2030 despite Chapter 11, local leaders say
players: WKMG reports local leaders in Brevard County say the Cocoa station is still expected to open in 2030, even after Brightline's parent entities filed Chapter 11. The operating company, Brightline Trains Florida, is not part of the filing and trains continue to run. I only saw the headline and summary of the Cocoa piece, not the full article.
why_it_matters: Local backing for the Orlando-to-Cocoa extension survives the filing, which keeps the station-led growth story alive on paper. But I did not see who funds it or how it fits with the restructuring, which cuts debt and brings $490m of new capital for the operator. Watch whether the plan sets aside money for expansion.
why_you_care: Your old deal: the extension and ridership upside you underwrote now depends on a funded restructuring, so check whether the plan keeps expansion capex before anyone at MSIP pitches Brightline-related angles.

headline: Meridiam closes $4.5bn North America Core Fund on demand above $7bn, built around 15 existing assets
players: Meridiam has closed its $4.5bn North America Core Fund. Total demand was above $7bn. The vehicle holds 15 assets in long-life transport and social infrastructure, drawn from the first two generations of Meridiam funds.
why_it_matters: The fund is seeded with existing Meridiam holdings, so it reads as a way to roll mature assets into a core vehicle and give earlier funds liquidity. That is my inference; the source does not call it a continuation fund. The oversubscription shows strong LP appetite for core, contracted transport and social assets. It is a useful read-across on how mature assets are being recycled and priced.
why_you_care: A fresh marker on core-asset demand and on how a peer recycles mature holdings, which bears on exit options for MSIP's transport and social assets.

headline: Bloomberg: Google nears multi-year nuclear power deal with Constellation worth $1bn or more; not yet announced
players: Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, citing people with knowledge, that Google is set to pay Constellation $1bn or more under a multi-year agreement. It could be announced this week. The location and scale of the nuclear capacity have not been reported, and neither company commented.
why_it_matters: This is a report, not a signed deal. If it lands, it would be another hyperscaler paying for output from existing reactors, which supports contracted cash flows on existing nuclear and the value of firm power near data centres. Watch for the contract tenor, whether it covers an uprate or only existing output, and any price disclosure, as these set comps for other nuclear and gas assets.
why_you_care: A $1bn-plus contract for existing nuclear output is a pricing and tenor marker for any firm-power or data-centre power thesis you work on at MSIP.

headline: Hess Midstream signs deal to buy Chevron's DJ Basin assets and Chevron's full stake in Hess Midstream; close targeted by year-end
players: Hess Midstream LP and Chevron signed a purchase and sale agreement on Oct 6. Hess Midstream will acquire Chevron's crude oil, gas and storage assets in Colorado's DJ Basin, plus Chevron's entire ownership of Hess Midstream and its general partner. Closing is targeted by year-end 2026. The report cites lower-tariff, long-term Bakken contracts, fixed-fee DJ Basin agreements and a shareholder-elected board from 2028. Price was not in the report I read; terms undisclosed here.
why_it_matters: The deal swaps a lower Bakken tariff for longer contracts and adds fixed-fee DJ Basin volumes with an investment-grade producer, so cash flow becomes more predictable but possibly thinner per barrel. Governance moves away from the parent. It is a template for how sponsor-style independence is priced in midstream. Watch for price disclosure and the pro forma leverage.
why_you_care: A midstream comp on contract length, tariff trade-offs and parent separation, useful when MSIP looks at gas infrastructure; background only until price is disclosed.

headline: Axium portfolio company UPPCO agrees to buy Xcel Energy's regulated electric utilities in Michigan
players: Axium Infrastructure said its wholly owned portfolio company Upper Peninsula Power Company (UPPCO) has agreed to acquire Xcel Energy's regulated electric transmission and distribution utilities in Michigan. The deal is pending regulatory approval. The page I read gave no price, so terms are undisclosed here.
why_it_matters: Regulated utilities earn an allowed return on rate base, so cash flows depend on commission decisions, not on demand. Here a sponsor-owned platform is buying from a listed parent, an add-on route that can bring scale and cost savings. With no price disclosed, there is no multiple to mark yet. Watch the Michigan approval process and the price relative to rate base.
why_you_care: Utility add-ons by sponsor-owned platforms are a live pricing and structuring comp for MSIP's utilities and power work; once a price emerges, check it against rate base.

headline: LS Power closes ~$6bn Fund VI at hard cap; ~$1.7bn already committed to Constellation gas plants
players: LS Power closed LS Power Equity Partners VI with about $6bn of commitments against an original $4bn target. The fund launched in January 2026 and was fully allocated by July. It is more than twice the $2.7bn Fund V, which closed in 2024 and is now fully deployed.
why_it_matters: A fund that hit its hard cap and was fully allocated within about six months shows LPs still back power-focused managers. About $1.7bn is already committed to pending purchases of Constellation gas plants, which would form a roughly 5 GW platform across PJM and ERCOT. Watch the price per kW on those deals and whether other sponsors chase the same gas assets.
why_you_care: LS Power is a power-focused rival with fresh capital and a gas platform in PJM and ERCOT, which overlaps MSIP's stated focus on power generation and natural gas; use it to gauge competition and pricing.

headline: Energy Transfer agrees to buy Vaquero Midstream for about $2.625bn in cash and units
players: Energy Transfer signed a definitive agreement to buy Vaquero Midstream in a bolt-on valued at about $2.625bn. Consideration is $1.95bn in cash plus about 33.3m new Energy Transfer common units. Vaquero owns a 300-mile pipeline network and a gas processing complex with 675 MMcf/d of capacity in the southern Delaware Basin, with acreage to expand to 1.2 bcf/d.
why_it_matters: A strategic buyer is paying for Permian gas processing that plugs into its own pipes and fractionation, which is where synergy value comes from. It sets a recent comp for Delaware Basin gas processing and shows strategics can outbid sponsors on connected assets. The EBITDA multiple was not in the sources I read. Watch for that and for closing conditions.
why_you_care: Natural gas is a core MSIP focus sector, and this is a fresh Permian processing comp, though a strategic one, so its synergies may not carry over to a sponsor's underwriting.

headline: Google and Constellation announce 20-year, 890 MW nuclear uprate PPA backed by $4.3bn of investment, plus 15-year, 2,700 MW supply deal
players: Constellation and Google announced a 20-year power purchase agreement for 890 MW of new nuclear capacity, delivered through uprates at 11 Constellation units in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Constellation says it will invest more than $4.3bn, and the first uprate is expected in 2028. A separate 15-year agreement covers another 2,700 MW from Constellation's existing PJM fleet. Price terms were not disclosed.
why_it_matters: This confirms the Bloomberg report of Oct 6 that we logged as a pending deal. A hyperscaler is now paying to expand existing reactors, not just buy their output. On my arithmetic, $4.3bn for 890 MW is about $4.8m per MW, but PPA pricing is undisclosed, so no return can be derived. Watch for price leaks and for PJM treatment of the new capacity.
why_you_care: It sets a fresh comp for what hyperscalers will fund on existing nuclear and for contracted power cash flows, useful when marking any power or data-centre-adjacent deal.

headline: LOGISTEC and Port of Corner Brook mark launch of NEAS liner service to Western Newfoundland; no financial terms
players: On Oct 5, the Port of Corner Brook and LOGISTEC, described as an Enstructure company, marked the launch of Nunavut Eastern Arctic Shipping's new liner service to Western Newfoundland. LOGISTEC says it operates in 62 ports and 85 terminals across Canada, the US and Mexico. No financial terms were given.
why_it_matters: This is operating news, not a transaction. It adds an Arctic-supply liner call at a LOGISTEC-served port, which supports volume diversification, but no revenue figure is given. For a terminal operator, value comes from throughput and long-term customer contracts rather than one new service. Watch for volume, contract or ownership news from the company.
why_you_care: Background only: a small operating update on a deal you worked at Rothschild, with nothing that changes the thesis or is worth raising at MSIP yet.

headline: Norway's NBIM commits €1.2bn to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners' new flagship renewables fund, CI VI
players: Norges Bank Investment Management committed €1.2bn (about $1.34bn) to CIP's CI VI fund, which invests mainly in renewable generation and storage across OECD markets. CIP is reportedly seeking €16bn for the fund; its predecessor, CIP V, closed in 2025 at €12bn. NBIM put €900m into CIP V in 2024.
why_it_matters: A single anchor ticket of this size shows big sovereign LPs are still writing large cheques for development-stage renewables despite the sector's wobbles. A €16bn reported target would be a third larger than CIP V, which means more dry powder bidding for wind, solar and storage platforms. Watch for the first close and how CIP prices its next deals.
why_you_care: CIP is a watchlist rival for renewable and storage platforms, so its fundraising pace is a read on competition and pricing for deals MSIP might look at.

headline: AD Ports completes $835m purchase of Brazil's CLI from Macquarie Asset Management and IG4 Capital
players: AD Ports Group has closed its purchase of Brazilian agri-bulk terminal operator CLI. The deal was announced June 2 at an enterprise value of AED 3.1bn (US$835m). Sellers were funds managed by Macquarie Asset Management and IG4 Capital. Brazil's ANTAQ and CADE approved it. CLI's Santos and Itaqui terminals handled 17m tonnes in 2025, with revenue of Dhs654m and EBITDA of Dhs360m.
why_it_matters: On the disclosed figures, EV to 2025 EBITDA works out to about 8.6x by my arithmetic. That is a usable comp for emerging-market port terminals with long-term port concessions. The buyer is a strategic, which shows how infrastructure funds exit port assets: sell to a port operator that gets operating synergies, not to another fund.
why_you_care: A completed port exit by Macquarie at roughly 8.6x EBITDA gives you a fresh strategic-buyer comp for port and terminal underwriting, and a read on what a strategic will pay.

headline: FTAI Infrastructure's $1.52bn Long Ridge sale now seen closing in Q4, slipping from a September target
players: FTAI Infrastructure signed a $1.52bn agreement to sell Long Ridge, which needs FERC approval. Its 10-Q estimated a September close; Citizens now expects the fourth quarter, with the asset on FIP's books through October. On the call, management said the sale should remove about $1.4bn of debt, over $1.1bn of it at Long Ridge, and ex-Long Ridge adjusted EBITDA hit a record $48.7m in Q2.
why_it_matters: Long Ridge takes roughly $100m of annual EBITDA out, per Citizens, against total debt of $2.89bn, so leverage falls but earnings shrink. The 10-Q ties the Jefferson bridge loan return to 1.19x for repayments through Oct 31; I did not see the rate after that. Delay past October could cost money. Watch the FERC approval date.
why_you_care: Your FTAI thesis now rests on Transtar, Jefferson and Repauno cash flow without Long Ridge; the closing timing and bridge-loan cost are worth watching as that deleveraging plays out.

headline: Brightline gets court approval to borrow $190m in bankruptcy financing, per Law360; figure differs from $258m interim DIP logged earlier
players: Law360 reported on Oct 5 that Brightline won approval to borrow $190m in bankruptcy financing. The parent entities filed Chapter 11 in late September under a restructuring support agreement; the operating company, Brightline Trains Florida, is not in the filing. I only saw the headline summary, so I cannot say why this differs from the $258m interim DIP already logged.
why_it_matters: The difference from the $258m interim figure matters because the DIP size sets how much runway the parent has before a plan is voted. The $490m of new long-term capital is the real fix; DIP money only buys time. Watch the final DIP order, the plan timetable and whether the numbers reconcile once the court docket is read.
why_you_care: Your Brightline deal is now in court; once the plan settles, check whether discounted debt or a rail-adjacent asset becomes a sourcing angle worth flagging at MSIP.

headline: NYT: data-centre and energy-supply IPOs are being delayed as Wall Street turns more sceptical
players: The New York Times reports the backlash against data centres is spilling into capital markets. Companies that house data centres or supply them with energy and land were expected to dominate the IPO market in coming months. One company that planned to list on Nasdaq last month, seeking up to $900m at a valuation of up to $10bn, has held back, and another has slowed its timing, per people briefed.
why_it_matters: A public-market exit is one of the ways sponsors underwrite data-centre and power-for-AI platforms. If IPO windows narrow, exits lean on trade sales and large private buyers, such as the reported Stack Asia-Pacific talks. That puts more weight on contracted cash flow and less on growth multiples. The excerpt does not name the companies or give a full list of delays.
why_you_care: It is a risk to exit assumptions for any digital or AI-power deal you underwrite at MSIP, so test returns with a private-buyer exit rather than an IPO.

headline: July infrastructure fundraising topped $28bn, per Alternatives Watch; Q1 2026 had been lowest first quarter since 2023
players: Alternatives Watch reports that private equity led July fundraising with more than $63bn, infrastructure managers closed over $28bn, and total fundraising topped $119bn. Separately, Institutional Real Estate, Inc. data showed 18 infrastructure funds closing $32.0bn in Q1 2026, the lowest first quarter since 2023, with no megafunds.
why_it_matters: One month at $28bn compares with $32bn for all of Q1, so capital is flowing again, led by large managers. More dry powder chasing data-centre and power assets likely supports prices. Q3 also includes KKR's $19.2bn fund close on Aug 3. Watch whether Q3 totals confirm a rebound or just a few large closes.
why_you_care: Fundraising backdrop for MSIP's own capital raising and for how much rivals can afford to bid; a pricing-pressure factor to carry into comps.

headline: We Energies offers Oracle 10-20% of Point Beach nuclear output for Port Washington data centre; files for new gas plant
players: On Oct 2, We Energies announced an agreement letting Oracle subscribe to 10% to 20% of Point Beach's generation. The power would serve Project Lighthouse, the Port Washington campus Oracle is co-developing with OpenAI. The same day, We Energies filed a separate application with the state PSC to build a gas plant at the Fox Energy Center site, which would more than double that site's output. The utility says the Point Beach proposal could save other customers millions in fuel costs.
why_it_matters: A regulated utility is selling a slice of an existing nuclear plant to a hyperscaler and also asking to build gas, so data-centre demand is being met with both nuclear and gas. The structure is a subscription, not a plant sale, which keeps the asset in the rate base. Regulatory approval and how the customer-savings claim is tested are the points to watch.
why_you_care: A utility-subscription structure for nuclear output, paired with a new gas build for the same load, is a template to compare against MSIP's power and utilities deal flow.

headline: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank closes second Japan infrastructure fund at ¥123bn
players: Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank reached a final close of ¥123bn (over $830m) for Japan Infrastructure No. 2, Limited Partnership. The fund was established Oct 1, 2025. It targets Japanese decarbonisation, social and digital infrastructure.
why_it_matters: It is small by global standards but shows domestic Japanese bank-sponsored capital building a dedicated infrastructure pool, which adds local competition for mid-sized Japanese assets. It is a data point on fundraising, which has been uneven this year. Watch for first deployments and whether global sponsors partner with it.
why_you_care: Background only: a local pool of Japanese infrastructure capital that could compete with, or co-invest alongside, MSIP in Asia-Pacific deals.

headline: Enerflex wins about 450 MW off-grid gas power order from unnamed data-centre developer; deliveries 2027-28
players: Enerflex will design, engineer, fabricate and assemble about 450 MW of behind-the-meter gas-fired generation for a North American data-centre developer it did not name. Deliveries start in 2027 and finish in 2028. Contract value was not disclosed. Enerflex also authorised about $85m to expand its Engineered Systems facilities, mostly in 2027, and its shares rose more than 10%.
why_it_matters: Enerflex is an equipment maker, so there is no contracted yield to underwrite here. The signal is that developers are paying for prime power that does not need a grid connection, and that equipment build slots are a real constraint. The aftermarket service tail is the recurring piece. Watch whether the developer later brings in an owner or financier for the units.
why_you_care: A fresh demand signal for off-grid gas power, the same gas-to-AI theme as Sisu/Miratech; equipment lead times are a risk to flag if MSIP underwrites behind-the-meter power.

headline: Trump says South Korea will invest $200bn in US energy, including eight reactors in a $120bn nuclear programme
players: Trump posted on Truth Social on Wednesday that South Korea will invest $200bn in US nuclear, LNG and natural gas infrastructure, following a meeting with President Lee Jae Myung at the UN General Assembly. He said it falls under the $350bn Korea Strategic Trade and Investment Deal reached last year. The source I read gives no project list, sponsors or timetable.
why_it_matters: This is a political announcement, not a financed project. If it firms up, it adds demand for LNG, gas pipes and nuclear supply chains, and it will compete for the same equipment and construction capacity infrastructure funds depend on. Treat it as a headline until named projects and funding structures appear.
why_you_care: Background for now: no project-level terms, but it could steer LNG, gas and nuclear deal flow toward the same assets rivals chase; Stonepeak already holds 40% of Woodside's Louisiana LNG.
